findings.title: 0.24 m/s is not a lower bound for short windows — the table can refuse a feasible config
findings.summary: The 400 entry (0.24 m/s) sits ABOVE the only ramp-inclusive measurement this project has at linear 400 (0.191 m/s over a 4 s average including ramp and stop, measured 2026-08-30 and cited in the constant's own comment). The comment at services.py:9530-9531 claims the table is "the slowest speed the mower has ever shown", which is false for total windows of roughly 3-6 s, where the ramp dominates and the mower averages well under 0.24 m/s. In that regime the check is an UPPER bound, not a lower one, and refuses configs that would complete inside the guard.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator runs a short first-light characterisation: baseline_ms 1000 / step_ms 1000 / settle_ms 1000 (total_ms 3000, all schema-legal) with a deliberately tight max_travel_m of 0.70. floor_travel_m = 0.24 * 3.0 = 0.72 > 0.70, so services.py:10105 appends step_window_travel_exceeds_budget and services.py:10145 returns before any command is sent. Actual travel at the measured ramp-inclusive ~0.19 m/s is ~0.57 m — the run fits the budget comfortably and is refused anyway, with a reason that names a budget overrun that would not have happened. Same shape at total_ms 5000 with max_travel_m 1.0 (floor 1.20 vs actual ~0.96).

findings.title: The blocker gives the intended 23 s / linear 300 run no protection, and the planning travel figure is a ramp-inclusive average applied to a sustained window
findings.summary: The 300 entry (0.10 m/s) is correctly a lower bound, so by construction it cannot fire for the intended run — the guard alone carries the censoring risk there. But the feasibility claim behind the change ("at 300 a 23 s window travels ~2.5 m") is derived from 0.116 m/s, itself a 4 s average including ramp and stop. At linear 400 the same 4 s ramp-inclusive figure (0.191) understates the sustained 15 s figure (0.2616) by 1.37x. Applying that factor to 300 gives ~0.16 m/s sustained and ~3.7 m over 23 s — 82% of the 4.5 m budget, not 56%. The guard also sums per-sample |chord| (services.py:7655), so ~23 samples of 2-4 cm position noise inflate cumulative_travel_m further. There is no sustained-speed measurement at linear 300 anywhere in the record.
findings.failure_scenario: The predeclared run dispatches (baseline 3000 / step 15000 / settle 5000, linear 300, max_travel_m 4.5). floor_travel_m = 0.10 * 23 = 2.3 <= 4.5, so no blocker fires. If sustained speed at 300 is ~0.19 m/s rather than the assumed ~0.11, cumulative_travel_m reaches 4.5 m at ~20 s — inside the 15 s step phase's own tail or the settle phase — and _apply_travel_guard trips max_travel_reached at services.py:7670, aborting the window. The settle phase is truncated, tau is censored, vio_analysis 2b has no carryover to measure, and a supervised run is spent — precisely the outcome the new blocker was added to prevent. Safety is unaffected (containment is gated at max_travel_m + 0.50 m independently).

findings.title: Unknown linear_speed silently falls back to the FAST speed's bound, with nothing tying the table to the schema
findings.summary: _STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR.get(int(linear_speed), 0.24) hard-codes the 400 entry as the fallback. Nothing links the dict's keys to STEP_RESPONSE_PROBE_SCHEMA's vol.In([300, 400]) (services.py:987) — no assertion, no test. A lookup miss is invisible: it produces a plausible number and no log line. This commit itself is the shape of the hazard: it widened vol.In and remembered the table; the next widening may not.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change admits linear_speed 500 in vol.In([300, 400, 500]) (services.py:987-988) without adding a 500 entry to the table. The mower does roughly 0.33 m/s at 500, but floor_travel_m uses 0.24, so a 15 s window at max_travel_m 4.5 computes 3.6 m and passes, while actual travel is ~4.95 m and trips the guard mid-window. The full test suite stays green because every test in tests/components/mammotion/test_step_response_probe.py exercises only 300 and 400. The mirror-image failure (admitting a slower speed, e.g. 200, and silently over-refusing every config with the 400 bound) is equally undetected.

result.notes:
Verified answers to the four questions asked.

DIRECTION — correct in intent and correct for long windows. floor_travel_m is a minimum-expected travel; the refusal fires only when even that minimum overruns max_travel_m, so marginal configs are left to the runtime guard. The one place the direction inverts is short windows at linear 400, where 0.24 exceeds the measured ramp-inclusive 0.191 m/s (finding 1). Note the design deliberately leaves a guaranteed-trip band unrefused: at the measured sustained 0.2616 m/s, any window over ~17.2 s at linear 400 will trip the guard, while refusal only begins at 18.75 s (0.24 * t > 4.5). That is consistent with the stated "lower bound" philosophy but means the blocker's stated purpose is only partly met at 400 too.

total_ms — yes, it is the sum of all three phases (services.py:10077), and that is the right quantity: _step_response_phase_scheduler (services.py:9666-9712) only ever writes command_state["angular_speed"]; linear_speed is set once at services.py:10249 and is never changed, so the mower drives at the commanded linear speed through baseline, step AND settle. The travel guard also measures the same quantity the blocker projects — cumulative consecutive-fix path length via math.hypot at services.py:7655, with no minimum-chord filter — so speed x time is dimensionally the right comparison, not an apples-to-oranges displacement check.

.get default — see finding 3. Unreachable via the service today (schema restricts to {300, 400} and the impl's own default is 400), so this is a latent maintenance hazard, not a live bug.

max_travel_m validity — guaranteed. STEP_RESPONSE_PROBE_SCHEMA constrains it to vol.Range(min=0.10, max=4.5) (services.py:1021-1023), handle_step_response_probe reads call.data["max_travel_m"] directly with no .get default (services.py:20156), the service is registered with that schema (services.py:21020), and _step_response_probe_impl's own default is _STEP_RESPONSE_DEFAULT_TRAVEL_M = 2.50. It is never 0 and is never a divisor.

GATING TRACE — the blocker does prevent dispatch, confirmed by reading the whole path. blockers is built at services.py:10087, appended at 10106, and the result dict at 10108 computes "would_send": not dry_run and not blockers AFTER the append. Then services.py:10145-10147: `if dry_run or blockers: result["reason"] = ...; return result`. Nothing between line 10106 and that return touches BLE — the first movement command is _send_manager_command_with_args at services.py:10259, well past it, and the sampler/phase/refresh tasks are created after that. The real-run wrapper _step_response_probe (services.py:10382) has no path that bypasses the impl. So a refused call commands no motion. One pre-existing side effect worth knowing (not introduced here): a refused REAL call has already taken the exclusive report lease, whose first act is RPT_STOP, and the finally block calls async_stop_continuous_reports — so a refusal still leaves the background report stream stopped until it restarts.

OUT-OF-DIMENSION observation, flagged not scored: at linear 300 the ~1 Hz chord is ~0.12-0.16 m against config.min_travel_for_heading_trust_m = 0.15 used at services.py:10347, so the RTK course_series/analysis will be largely or entirely non-informative on the intended run. That is acceptable under rule E-VIO (RTK is diagnostics only), but it means the run that motivates this change loses the independent RTK cross-check — the very instrument that surfaced the VIO/RTK disagreement on 2026-08-30.

result.reasoning:
REFUTED on three independent grounds.

**1. The fallback branch is unreachable in this code.** `_step_response_probe_impl` (services.py:10053) is reached only via `_step_response_probe` (services.py:10382), whose sole caller is `handle_step_response_probe` (services.py:20137-20144), registered at services.py:21020 with `schema=STEP_RESPONSE_PROBE_SCHEMA`. HA validates against that schema before the handler is invoked, and `vol.All(vol.Coerce(int), vol.In([300, 400]))` (services.py:986-988) guarantees `int(linear_speed)` is 300 or 400 at services.py:10101. The `.get(..., 0.24)` default is dead today. There is no present-tense defect — the claim is about a hypothetical future edit.

**2. The claim's load-bearing factual premise is false.** It states "The full test suite stays green because every test in tests/components/mammotion/test_step_response_probe.py exercises only 300 and 400." It does not. tests/components/mammotion/test_step_response_probe.py:745-747 (added by THIS commit) reads:

    for rejected in (0, 200, 350, 500):
        with pytest.raises(vol.Invalid):
            _validated(linear_speed=rejected)

Widening `vol.In` to `[300, 400, 500]` makes `_validated(linear_speed=500)` return successfully, so `pytest.raises(vol.Invalid)` fails and the suite goes RED. The mirror-image case the claim names (admitting 200) is pinned by the same loop. Both of the exact scenarios the claim describes as "undetected" are detected. The schema's admissible set is pinned; a maintainer widening it must edit this very test, which is the moment they are looking directly at the speed constraint.

**3. Even granting the hypothetical, the consequence is not a safety defect — it is the status quo ante.** The gate is explicitly documented as a measurement-quality gate, not a containment gate (services.py:10093-10098): "a wasted supervised run rather than an unsafe one... a marginal config is left to the guard, which is what actually carries the safety." The claimed failure ("trips the guard mid-window") is precisely the pre-existing designed behavior that every step-probe config had before this commit. The in-window sampler doubles as the travel guard and aborts at the UNCHANGED `max_travel_m` 4.5 ceiling, and `step_path_contained` (services.py:9642-9660) independently requires `max_travel_m + stop_overshoot_m` of clearance in EVERY direction — neither touched by this commit. A missing table entry degrades to "the guard does its job", it does not create exposure. Directionally: a fallback for a faster speed under-refuses into the guard (designed fallback); a fallback for a slower speed over-refuses and blocks the run (fail-closed, annoying not hazardous). Neither path produces uncontained motion.

What remains is a maintainability observation about a magic-number default, and even that is materially weaker than claimed given the pinning test at line 745. It does not meet the bar for a defect in this code.

REFUTED on both halves.

(1) "Gives the intended run no protection" is the documented design, not a defect. services.py:9528-9536 and 10093-10105 state the table is a LOWER bound so the blocker fires only on the impossible pairing, with the in-window guard carrying safety. Verified it does the job it claims: at linear 400, floor_travel = 0.24 * 23 = 5.52 > 4.5, so the long-window/fast-speed pairing is refused (refusal threshold 18.75 s at 400). At 300 the threshold is 45 s, beyond the 23 s cap set by _STEP_RESPONSE_MAX_TOTAL_MS — a known, stated consequence of rounding down.

(2) The claimed failure scenario contradicts its own numbers. The claim's corrected sustained estimate at 300 (0.116 * 1.37 = 0.159 m/s) gives 0.159 * 23 = 3.65 m, comfortably under the 4.5 m guard — no trip. Tripping within the 23 s window requires >= 4.5/23 = 0.196 m/s sustained at 300 (and "4.5 m at ~20 s" requires ~0.225 m/s). That demands a 1.69x ramp factor at 300 where the observed factor at 400 was 1.37x, and puts 300 at 75-86% of 400's sustained 0.2616 m/s when the only same-method A/B (4 s ramp-inclusive both sides, 2026-08-30) measured 0.116/0.191 = 61%. The scenario is unsupported by any measurement in the record and is inconsistent with the claim's own extrapolation.

(3) Noise inflation is immaterial. _apply_travel_guard (services.py:7652-7668) accumulates one chord only when position_sample.sequence == last+1, i.e. ~23 times at the ~1 Hz feed over a 23 s window, not once per 100 ms sample. Perpendicular noise adds in quadrature to a ~0.16 m chord: even at a pessimistic 3 cm sigma that is ~2.8 mm per sample, ~6 cm total, against ~0.85 m of remaining margin. Position noise during continuous motion was separately measured sub-cm (0.70 cm cross-track RMS); the 2-4 cm figure is a pulsed/stationary artifact.

(4) No safety exposure either way. Containment is gated at services.py:9626 as max_travel_m + stop_overshoot_m = 4.5 + 0.50 = 5.0 m of clearance in EVERY direction from the live position, computed independently of speed and of the new blocker, and max_travel_m's ceiling is unchanged at 4.5 (services.py:1021). A speed-estimate error therefore cannot move the exposure bound; it can only end the window earlier than planned. That outcome is explicitly registered in the predeclaration §4 ("guard trip ... FAIL. Not a smaller number"), and the intended run uses a 10.0 m square corridor against a ~5.9 m requirement.

Residual: the change does rest on an extrapolated rather than directly measured sustained speed at linear 300 — but that is a research-planning uncertainty with a registered FAIL outcome and roughly 0.85 m of guard headroom on the best available estimate, not a defect in this code.

REFUTED on the claim's own arithmetic, plus three independent grounds.

1. The failure scenario does not close. Window total = 3000+15000+5000 = 23.0 s; _apply_travel_guard trips at cumulative >= max_travel_m (services.py:7669), so a trip needs a whole-window mean speed (ramp from standstill included) of >= 4.5/23 = 0.196 m/s. The claim's OWN scaled estimate (0.116 x 1.37 = 0.159 m/s) gives 3.65 m — 19% margin, no trip. Its asserted 0.19 m/s gives 0.19 x 23 = 4.37 m — still no trip. Its stated "reaches 4.5 m at ~20 s" implies 0.225 m/s, which is 86% of the measured sustained speed at linear 400 (0.2616 m/s) and contradicts the one direct measurement at 300 that the claim itself cites (400 -> 0.191, 300 -> 0.116 on matched 4 s averages: a 25% command cut produced a 39% speed cut, i.e. worse than linear, so scaling sustained 0.2616 by the same factor gives ~0.16 m/s, not 0.196+).

2. The noise term is ~an order of magnitude short. The guard does accumulate per distinct ~1 Hz position sample (services.py:7736-7745 does one get_nowait() per 100 ms tick and _apply_travel_guard returns early on None), so ~23 accumulations. Closing 3.65 -> 4.5 m needs +37 mm of pure inflation per accumulation — larger than the entire 2-4 cm floor invoked. For isotropic sigma on a ~0.16 m chord only the perpendicular component inflates, second order: sigma^2/chord at sigma=0.03 is ~5.6 mm/interval ~= 0.13 m total; the project's own continuous-motion figure (0.70 cm cross-track RMS) gives ~7 mm. Pessimistic stack: 3.78 m against 4.5 m.

3. "No protection for the intended run" is the documented, deliberate contract, not a defect. services.py:9528-9538 and 10094-10099 both state the table is a LOWER bound that "fires only when the window cannot fit even at the slowest speed measured; a marginal config is left to the guard, which is what actually carries the safety", the predeclaration says the same, and a regression test pins it (test_the_travel_refusal_does_not_tighten_the_existing_defaults). The claim itself concedes safety is unaffected.

4. The ramp-inclusive figure never reaches the code's sizing path. "~2.5 m" is doc prose (docs/phase2-long-step-slow-speed-predeclared-20260901.md:42). The code sizes with _PROBE_SPEED_PER_LINEAR_UNIT_MS = 7.0e-04, rounded UP on purpose (services.py:900-904): at linear 300 over 23 s that is clock_bound_m 4.83 m and corridor_must_cover_m = max(4.5+0.50, 4.83) = 5.0 m (services.py:7931-7953) — above every speed the claim posits.

5. The stated consequence is overstated regardless: 2a is scored on the step phase (services.py:9982), which ends at 18 s, so even a hypothetical 20 s trip leaves the entire purpose of the commit intact; only 2b's tail thins.

Legitimate residue, not a code defect: there is genuinely no sustained-speed measurement at linear 300 anywhere in the record, and the doc's "~2.5 m" is optimistic. The code's conservative sizing constant already absorbs that gap, and no code path produces the claimed censoring.

The arithmetic is right and the defect is not. Verified in the real code: services.py:9538 defines {300: 0.10, 400: 0.24}; services.py:10100-10105 computes floor_travel_m = table[linear_speed] * total_ms/1000 and appends step_window_travel_exceeds_budget when it exceeds max_travel_m; services.py:10145 returns before any dispatch. Schema minimums (baseline/step/settle each min 1000 ms, max_travel_m min 0.10) do make the claimed total_ms 3000 / max_travel_m 0.70 config legal, and 0.24*3.0 = 0.72 > 0.70 does fire the blocker. So the mechanics of the claim reproduce.

It is still not a bug, for six reasons.

(1) The error direction is fail-closed, which is the correct direction on a real open-loop curved drive. A too-high table entry can only REFUSE a window; it can never dispatch one that should have been refused. The gates that carry actual safety are untouched: step_path_contained (max_travel_m + 0.50 m clearance in every direction, services.py:9626) and the in-window cumulative travel guard (services.py:7670, 10291). The code states this intent at 10096-10099: "a marginal config is left to the guard, which is what actually carries the safety." The claim is arguing for a looser pre-dispatch bound on a real mower.

(2) The refusal costs nothing and is visible before authorization. blockers is computed before the dry_run early return, so a dry run surfaces step_window_travel_exceeds_budget at zero cost. No supervised run is wasted and no mower is stranded.

(3) The invented scenario cannot produce a measurement anyway. baseline 1000 / step 1000 / settle 1000 sits at the schema floor on all three phases. This project's own banked numbers put onset lag at ~1-2 s and tau at 2.6-3.6 s, and services.py:1011-1012 states the design constraint: "The settle phase IS the experiment: it must outlast the carryover it is measuring, or tau is censored." A 1000 ms step does not clear onset; a 1000 ms settle cannot outlast tau. The gate is not depriving the operator of a usable experiment, which is what the claim's severity rests on.

(4) The claim's "actual ~0.57 m, fits comfortably" is computed from a figure the probe's own window does not reproduce. The 0.191 m/s number is a 4 s average INCLUDING ramp AND STOP (2026-08-30). The step probe drives baseline->step->settle continuously and stops only after the window, so removing the stop deceleration raises the in-window average. Against the 0.2616 m/s 15 s ramp-inclusive figure cited in the same comment, a 3 s from-standstill window plausibly covers ~0.6 m against a 0.70 m budget - inside the ~0.20 m minimum post-trip travel that _PROBE_TRAVEL_GUARD_OVERSHOOT_M's own derivation documents (services.py:885-894). The config is marginal, not comfortable; the claim's margin is smaller than the uncertainty in its own estimate.

(5) The operator must hand-set an unmotivated max_travel_m. The default is 2.50 (_STEP_RESPONSE_DEFAULT_TRAVEL_M). At the intended 10 m corridor, lowering it to 0.70 buys nothing - it only reduces the clearance step_path_contained demands, which is already satisfied at 4.5 + 0.50. Nothing in the service, schema, or predeclaration points an operator at 0.70.

(6) Where the gate actually fires, 0.24 is a genuine lower bound and the loosest defensible value was already chosen. Computed the firing envelope: at linear 400 with max_travel_m 4.5 the gate fires only above 18.75 s, where the measured speed is ~0.2616 m/s - so there it UNDER-refuses (errs toward permitting), exactly as intended. The schema defaults (10 s at 400, budget 2.50) pass at 2.40 with 0.10 m spare; 0.24 was picked precisely so the gate does not tighten pre-existing behaviour, and test_the_travel_refusal_does_not_tighten_the_existing_defaults pins that. The 300 entry (0.10 vs a measured 0.116 ramp-inclusive) is a true lower bound, and 300 is the speed the intended run uses.

What survives is a comment-wording nit, not a defect: "the slowest speed the mower has ever shown" (services.py:9530-9531) is loose for sub-8 s windows. But the same comment prints the exact figures the claim says are misrepresented (400 -> 0.191 m/s and 300 -> 0.116 m/s at 4 s; 0.2616 m/s at 15 s), so nothing is concealed from a reader, and the imprecision has no reachable consequence on any real run.

REFUTED — the claim describes a hypothetical future edit, not a defect in this code, and even its own failure scenario stops at the real safety mechanism.

(a) The fallback is unreachable. The sole entry point registers with `schema=STEP_RESPONSE_PROBE_SCHEMA` (services.py:21013-21021), which pins `vol.All(vol.Coerce(int), vol.In([300, 400]))` (services.py:986-988). At services.py:10101 `linear_speed` is therefore exactly 300 or 400, both of which are table keys; `.get(..., 0.24)` is dead code today. Coerce runs before In, so the new services.yaml select emitting "300"/"400" still normalizes to int keys. `_step_response_probe` (10382-10415) forwards the same validated kwargs.

(b) No safety consequence even in the hypothetical. The claimed end-state is "trips the guard mid-window" — that guard, `_step_response_travel_guard` (services.py:7621-7670), integrates MEASURED consecutive-fix path length and sets `travel_abort` at `max_travel_m` without ever consulting `_STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR`, so a bad speed estimate cannot widen it. Containment is separately enforced by `step_path_contained` (services.py:9626-9646), requiring `max_travel_m + stop_overshoot_m` (5.0 m) of clearance in every direction. The worst outcome is a censored measurement / wasted supervised run — precisely what the code comment at services.py:10093-10099 states the gate exists to prevent, explicitly noting the guard "is what actually carries the safety."

(c) The fallback direction is the more conservative of the two known entries: 0.24 is the LARGER value, so an unlisted speed gets the more-refusing bound. It under-refuses only for a speed faster than 400, and 400 is the fastest this project has ever commanded, with linear_speed documented as deliberately pinned and any raise treated as a stated safety trade.

(d) The mirror-image case (admitting 200, over-refusing at the 0.24 bound) is fail-closed — a spurious refusal commands no motion.

This is a maintainability/future-proofing suggestion about an edit nobody has made, not a concrete defect in the diff under review.

result.dimension: is linear_speed=300 correct end to end?
result.notes:
Verified clean (no finding needed):

1. **select selector -> schema coercion works.** `services.yaml:874-879` emits string options `"300"/"400"`; `vol.All(vol.Coerce(int), vol.In([300,400]))` accepts `"300"`, `"400"`, `300`, `400` (checked directly against the installed voluptuous). Identical to the already-shipped `step_angular_speed` pattern (services.yaml:884-892), so the yaml form is precedented and correct.

2. **300 really is plumbed to the wire, unclamped.** `handle_step_response_probe` (services.py:20147) -> `_step_response_probe_impl` -> `command_state = {"linear_speed": linear_speed, ...}` (services.py:10247) -> the opening `send_movement` -> `_continuous_refresh_window` re-reads `command_state["linear_speed"]` verbatim on every 200 ms refresh write. `_send_manager_command_with_args` applies no scaling, clamping or app-scale conversion. No literal 400 anywhere in the step-probe path.

3. **`_PROBE_SPEED_PER_LINEAR_UNIT_MS` is NOT used by this probe.** It belongs to `raw_pymammotion_motion_probe`'s `corridor_must_cover_m`/`clock_bound_m` (services.py:7931-7952). The step probe's containment gate `step_path_contained` (services.py:9640-9660) is speed-independent — `max_travel_m + stop_overshoot_m` — so there is no stale-400 corridor assumption to fix.

4. **The commit's central justification checks out.** `_step_response_vio_intervals` (services.py:9849) keys off consecutive *distinct* VIO headings and applies no chord/travel floor, so the 2026-08-30 objection to 300 (0.15 m RTK chord) genuinely does not transfer to the E-VIO scoring path. `_step_response_vio_analysis` has no baseline-phase dependency, so a slower straight baseline does not make the run unscoreable.

5. **300 is above the straight-line linear actuation deadband** — measured 0.116 m/s on 2026-08-30 (CLAUDE.md / docs/phase2-route1-predeclared-20260830.md:64-68). ⚠️ but see finding 3: that measurement is straight-line only and has no committed evidence file.

findings.title: step_window_travel_exceeds_budget cannot fire at linear 300 for the very config it exists to protect
findings.summary: _STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR[300] = 0.10 m/s is 14% below the only 300 measurement that exists (0.116 m/s) and ~37% below the sustained speed implied by the commit's own 400 ramp-vs-window ratio, so at linear 300 the new pre-dispatch refusal has no discriminating power and lets through exactly the window/guard pairing it was written to catch.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator calls raw_pymammotion_step_response_probe with the predeclared run — linear_speed 300, baseline 3000 / step 15000 / settle 5000 — but leaves max_travel_m at its schema default of 2.50 instead of typing 4.5. floor_travel_m = 0.10 * 23 = 2.30 <= 2.50, so step_window_travel_exceeds_budget does NOT fire (confirmed by running _step_response_probe: blockers came back without it). The run dispatches. At the commit's own measured 0.116 m/s the mower covers 2.67 m and the travel guard trips at ~21.6 s, censoring the settle phase (2b and tau). At the sustained speed implied by the same comment's 400 figures (0.191 m/s over 4 s vs 0.2616 m/s over a full window = 1.37x, giving ~0.159 m/s at 300) it trips at 15.7 s — inside the step phase, censoring criterion 2a itself. Either way it is a guard trip, which the predeclaration declares a FAIL, and the supervised daylight run is wasted. Contrast linear 400, where the same 23 s window IS correctly refused.

findings.title: strings.json still tells the operator linear_speed is "Fixed at the measured value 400", and it outranks the new services.yaml text
findings.summary: The service-field description in strings.json and translations/en.json was not updated, and Home Assistant resolves service field name/description from translations in preference to services.yaml — so the new services.yaml prose documenting 300 never renders, and the UI actively states the opposite of what the schema now accepts.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator opens Developer Tools -> Actions -> "Raw PyMammotion step response probe" on the deployed beta96 to set up the predeclared 300 run. The Linear speed field renders its description from component.mammotion.services.raw_pymammotion_step_response_probe.fields.linear_speed.description — "Forward command. Fixed at the measured value 400." The carefully written services.yaml:870-876 text explaining that 300 is admissible under E-VIO, and the step_ms text naming the new step_window_travel_exceeds_budget refusal, are dead and unreachable. An operator following the UI concludes 300 is not allowed, or picks it while believing the field is pinned. Note also that the two inline name:/description: blocks added by this commit are the ONLY two in the whole 5000-line services.yaml — every other field in this repo documents itself through strings.json, so the commit wrote the text into the one place the UI ignores. strings.json's step_ms description is likewise silent on the new 15000 ms ceiling.

findings.title: The (linear 300, angular +/-180) arc is unmeasured — 300 was measured only straight, and the schema's own neighbouring comment forbids this reasoning for the other axis
findings.summary: The only evidence for 300 is a 4 s straight-line probe at angular 0 (0.116 m/s), with no committed evidence file anywhere in docs/ — grep for '"linear_speed": 300' returns nothing. The intended run drives 300 simultaneously with angular +/-180, an operating point never exercised, while the step_angular_speed field four lines below refuses unmeasured values precisely because they "may sit in an actuation deadband".
findings.failure_scenario: The step probe drives an arc (linear and angular together), and there is a documented deadband at angular 180 when linear is 0 ("angular_speed_fast defaults to 180, in the stationary deadband"); linear 300 sits closer to that case than the measured 400. If the mower's yaw response at (300, 180) differs from (400, 180) — either because a track drops below actuation or simply because rotation rate depends on linear speed, which the predeclaration itself registers as unmeasured — then the entire justification for step_ms 15000 collapses: the k >= 7 requirement was derived from a 10.43 deg/s onset contamination measured at linear 400, and that magnitude does not transfer. The supervised run then either fails 2a again for a reason the model did not predict, or returns a tau that cannot be compared to the four banked 400 runs. The code comment admitting 300 (services.py:979-985) rebuts only the chord objection and carries none of this caveat, so a future reader sees "the objection does not transfer" with no mention that the operating point is new.

findings.title: At linear 300 the retained RTK cross-check diagnostic goes dark by construction
findings.summary: _step_response_course_series is still called with min_chord_m = config.min_travel_for_heading_trust_m (0.15 m). At 300 the ~1 Hz position chord is ~0.12-0.16 m, straddling that floor, so the RTK series that beta95 deliberately kept as the independent cross-check produces few or no informative intervals — silently, with no blocker and no field saying so.
findings.failure_scenario: The predeclared 300 run completes and scores cleanly under E-VIO. Its result carries "analysis": {"omega_step_deg_per_s": null, "rotation_after_zero_deg": null, "tau_actuator_s": null} because _step_response_analysis._rate needs >= 2 informative step rows and got 0-1, and every course_series[*].course_degrees is null. The run therefore has no independent instrument at all — exactly the RTK-vs-VIO cross-check that on 2026-08-30/31 reframed both published +120 and +180 verdicts and motivated rule E-VIO in the first place. Nothing in the schema, the yaml, or the predeclaration warns that choosing 300 buys the long step at the cost of the cross-check, so the null analysis block will read as a bug rather than a designed consequence.

findings.title: _STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR.get() silently falls back to the FAST speed's bound for any speed not in the table
findings.summary: The dict lookup defaults to 0.24 — the 400 entry — rather than failing loudly, so the two admissible-speed lists (vol.In in the schema and the keys of the speed table) can drift apart with no test or type error catching it.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change adds a third measured speed to vol.In([200, 300, 400]) at services.py:987 and forgets to add 200 to _STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR. A caller then requests linear_speed 200 with baseline 3000 / step 15000 / settle 5000 and max_travel_m 4.5: floor_travel_m = 0.24 * 23 = 5.52 > 4.5, so step_window_travel_exceeds_budget refuses a window that would actually travel roughly 1.8 m — reintroducing precisely the over-refusal regression the commit message says a first version already made and that test_the_travel_refusal_does_not_tighten_the_existing_defaults exists to pin. A KeyError, or a startup assertion that set(_STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR) equals the schema's allowed set, would fail loudly instead.

findings.title: Raising the total-window cap collapses the redundancy between the distance guard and the containment disk at linear 400
findings.summary: With _STEP_RESPONSE_MAX_TOTAL_MS at 23000 the new speed table still admits linear 400 up to 18750 ms at max_travel_m 4.5, whose clock-bound travel (18.75 s x 0.2616 m/s = 4.91 m) now sits within 0.09 m of the step_path_contained radius of 5.00 m, where the old 16000 ms cap left 0.81 m.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator picks linear_speed 400 with baseline 3750 / step 14000 / settle 1000 (18750 ms) and max_travel_m 4.5. floor_travel_m = 0.24 * 18.75 = 4.50, not greater than 4.5, so step_window_travel_exceeds_budget does not fire. If the cumulative-distance guard fails to accumulate correctly — the failure mode the containment disk is the last-line backstop for — the wall clock stops the run only after ~4.91 m of open-loop curved travel against a corridor proven to hold 5.00 m, leaving 9 cm of margin on a path whose shape is the unknown under test. Before this commit the same failure left 81 cm.

result.reasoning:
REFUTATION FAILED — the claim is confirmed, and the supporting evidence is stronger than the claim states.

WHAT THE CODE DOES (verified, not assumed)
- custom_components/mammotion/services.py:9538 `_STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR = {300: 0.10, 400: 0.24}`, documented at :9529-9537 as "the slowest speed the mower has ever shown", rounded DOWN "on purpose", so that "a merely MARGINAL config still dispatches and only an impossible one is refused."
- services.py:10100-10106 computes `floor_travel_m = table[linear_speed] * total_ms/1000` and appends `step_window_travel_exceeds_budget` when `floor_travel_m > max_travel_m`; :10145 `if dry_run or blockers: return result` — the run is refused pre-dispatch.
- The guard the projection models is cumulative PATH length (services.py:7655 `guard_state["cumulative_distance_m"] += math.hypot(...)`, :7670 trip test), so `floor_travel_m` and `max_travel_m` are the same physical quantity. The comparison is dimensionally sound; only the constant is wrong.
- Its regression test `test_the_travel_refusal_does_not_tighten_the_existing_defaults` pins the lower-bound intent, but only at ONE point: the schema defaults (10 s, 2.50 m → floor 2.40, a 4% margin). It does not test the invariant it claims to protect.

THE CONSTANT IS NOT A LOWER BOUND — measured from this repo's own raw samples
I computed the cumulative-travel rate (the exact guard metric) from all five banked step-probe runs at linear_speed 400, docs/raw-samples/*.json:
  run1 (13.0 s):        2.7111 m → 0.2085 m/s
  run1repeat (13.0 s):  2.7732 m → 0.2133 m/s
  run2 +180 (15.0 s):   2.9536 m → 0.1969 m/s
  run2repeat (15.0 s):  3.8730 m → 0.2582 m/s
  stepext (15.0 s):     2.9020 m → 0.1934 m/s
FOUR OF FIVE full-window averages are BELOW 0.24 m/s; the minimum is 0.1934 m/s, 19% below the "lower bound". Only run2repeat (0.2582, the run cited in the constant's own comment as "0.2616 m/s over a full 15 s window") sits above it. So the constant is roughly the MAXIMUM of the population, not the minimum — the comment at :9530-9531 is false against the project's own evidence, at every window length, not just short ones.

At short horizons it is far worse. Measured cumulative travel at ~3000 ms elapsed, across the same five runs: 0.454, 0.458, 0.226, 0.306, 0.201 m. The gate's floor for a 3 s window is 0.720 m — 57%-258% above every real measurement.

THE FALSE REFUSAL IS REAL — executed, not reasoned
I ran `_step_response_probe` against the shipped code (temporary test, since removed). All configs below are schema-legal and all are refused with `step_window_travel_exceeds_budget`:
  1000/1000/1000, lin 400, max_travel 0.70  → floor 0.720 > 0.70  REFUSED (measured 3 s travel 0.20-0.46 m)
  1000/2000/2000, lin 400, max_travel 1.00  → floor 1.200 > 1.00  REFUSED (measured 5 s travel 0.66-1.22 m)
  3000/3000/4000, lin 400, max_travel 2.00  → floor 2.400 > 2.00  REFUSED (measured 10 s travel 1.78-2.38 m; 4 of 5 runs ≤2.07)
  3000/5000/5000, lin 400, max_travel 3.00  → floor 3.120 > 3.00  REFUSED
The last one is the strongest counter-example and is not hypothetical: it is a byte-for-byte replay of banked route-1 run 1 / run 1 repeat, both of which COMPLETED their full window at 2.7111 m and 2.7732 m — comfortably inside 3.00 m with ~0.23 m to spare. The new gate refuses a re-run of an already-executed, already-contained configuration at a budget tighter than the 4.00 m originally used. That is precisely the "refuses a feasible config" behaviour the commit message and the regression test say was eliminated.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND A NUISANCE (the part the claim understates)
The gate is fail-closed, so nothing unsafe dispatches — but the natural operator workaround for `step_window_travel_exceeds_budget` is to RAISE `max_travel_m`, which is the bound that actually carries the safety and which drives `step_path_contained`'s required clearance (`max_travel_m + 0.50 m` in every direction, services.py:9626). A projection that over-states travel therefore pressures the operator to loosen the real guard and demand more corridor. It also inverts the stated design contract that "the travel guard, not a projection, keeps carrying the safety."

SCOPE / WHAT IS NOT AFFECTED
The intended run (3000/15000/5000, linear 300, max_travel 4.5) is unaffected: floor 2.30 ≤ 4.5. The 400-speed runs at max_travel 4.0/4.5 also pass (13 s floor 3.12, 15 s floor 3.60). So this blocks no currently-planned work — which is why this is a correctness/documentation defect rather than a blocker.

FIX: set the 400 entry to at most the measured minimum (≈0.19, or ~0.17 with margin) and correct the comment at :9529-9537, which asserts a fact the banked data refutes. Consider also pinning the invariant empirically (a test that the table entry is ≤ the slowest banked full-window rate) rather than at the single default point.

REFUTED. The claim is factually correct that no run has ever exercised (linear 300, angular ±180) together, but every consequence it draws is either already registered in writing by this same commit or is structurally impossible.

1. THE CAVEAT IS REGISTERED VERBATIM, IN THIS COMMIT. The claim's core assertion is that the new operating point is unregistered and a future reader will not see it. `docs/phase2-long-step-slow-speed-predeclared-20260901.md` is ADDED BY COMMIT 20209385 ITSELF (94 lines, in the stat), and its §4 closes with: "⚠️ Registered before the run: `linear_speed` 300 is a **different operating point**, so results are NOT directly comparable to the four banked runs at 400, and the rotation rate at +180 may itself depend on linear speed — that is unmeasured. **Do not merge this run into the n-count of the 400 runs.**" That is the claimed risk, stated before dispatch, in the document the commit message names. §6.2 additionally registers that step_ms 15000 is "necessary but NOT sufficient" and that "a 2a FAIL on this run must NOT be read as 'the plant is not steady'." The claim's stated harm — an uncomparable τ, or a 2a FAIL misread — is pre-empted by the predeclaration's own outcome table.

2. THE DEADBAND ANALOGY IS A CATEGORY ERROR THE PROJECT HAS ALREADY CORRECTED. The neighbouring `step_angular_speed` comment (services.py:989-993) refuses values BELOW the measured ANGULAR band (120-180). This change leaves that field untouched at [-180,-120,120,180] — every admissible angular value is inside its measured band. The linear axis at 300 is likewise a MEASURED, actuating value (0.116 m/s, 2026-08-30); it was eliminated on an INSTRUMENT ground (below the 0.15 m RTK chord floor), never a deadband ground, and E-VIO removes exactly that floor. So neither axis is outside its measured band and the comment is not being contradicted. The specific deadband the claim invokes ("angular_speed_fast defaults to 180, in the stationary deadband") is documented as STATIONARY-ONLY: CLAUDE.md records "'Angular needs 500' is a STATIONARY-only finding — 180 actuated fine in an arc; the 2026-07-25 A/B measured a pure in-place turn," corroborated by docs/arcs-work-20260812.md:17 (`linear 400, angular 180` → 0.5823 m, +22.20°). Arguing that linear 300 "sits closer to" linear 0 than 400 does is the exact linear-extrapolation reasoning this project already refuted in writing ("A 25% command cut produced a 39% speed cut — the relationship is NOT linear").

3. NO SAFETY CONSEQUENCE — CONTAINMENT IS CURVATURE-AGNOSTIC BY CONSTRUCTION. This is the decisive point under the real-mower lens. `_apply_travel_guard` (services.py:7652-7671) accumulates `math.hypot` between CONSECUTIVE samples, i.e. PATH LENGTH, which is ≥ true displacement for any curve. `step_path_contained` (services.py:9625-9646) requires `max_travel_m + stop_overshoot_m` of clearance in EVERY direction, with the code comment stating the reason outright: "The open-loop path is curved and its exact shape is the UNKNOWN this probe exists to measure, so no direction may be assumed: require the whole disk." `max_travel_m` is UNCHANGED at 4.5. Therefore whatever the (300,180) yaw response turns out to be — under-actuating and driving straight, over-actuating and pivoting tight, or one track stalling entirely — displacement is bounded by 4.5 m of path against 5.0 m of required clearance. The unmeasured yaw response cannot reach the safety bound.

4. THE SLOWER SPEED MOVES THE GUARD IN THE CONSERVATIVE DIRECTION. At 300 the ~1 Hz chords are smaller, so the 2-4 cm position noise the predeclaration §6.1 flags inflates `cumulative_travel_m` relative to true displacement MORE than at 400. That makes the guard trip EARLIER than true travel warrants — a wasted run, never an overrun.

5. RESIDUAL IS A COMMENT-SCOPE NIT, NOT A DEFECT. The comment at services.py:979-985 is scoped to why 300 became admissible (the chord objection) and cites the findings doc; it makes no claim that the combined operating point is measured, so there is nothing false to mislead a reader. The step_angular_speed warning sits four lines below, unmodified and visible to the same reader, and the registered caveat lives in the predeclaration shipped in the same commit. Worst case here is measurement quality on a supervised, per-run-authorized, daylight run — which the predeclaration already scores as a FAIL rather than "a smaller number."

REFUTED — the claim is an experiment-design/documentation objection whose physical premise is contradicted by the repo's own measurements, and whose consequence is already registered in writing before dispatch.

1. The comment's actual claim is narrower than the claim asserts, and is true. services.py:979-985 says exactly one thing: the objection that eliminated 300 on 2026-08-30 — the RTK course statistic's 0.15 m chord floor — does not transfer under rule E-VIO, which reads VIO heading between consecutive distinct readings and imposes no travel floor. That is correct, and it is precisely scoped. The comment nowhere claims (300, ±180) is a characterised operating point.

2. The deadband analogy is inverted, and the repo says so. The documented deadband is the ANGULAR axis at ZERO linear — static friction on an in-place pivot ("angular_speed_fast defaults to 180, in the stationary deadband"). CLAUDE.md records the direct A/B refuting the transfer: "'Angular needs 500' is a STATIONARY-only finding — 180 actuated fine in an arc" (2026-08-12, linear 400 + angular 180 rotated course +22.20° over 0.5823 m). linear 300 is measured to translate at 0.116 m/s (2026-08-30), so the mower is not stationary and static friction is already broken; a lower linear command does not move the machine toward the stationary case. On a differential drive the wheel-speed DIFFERENCE (which sets ω) is the angular command; linear is the common-mode term. Lowering it tightens the arc radius — more yaw per metre, not less actuation.

3. The "neighbouring comment forbids this for the other axis" argument fails on its face: the commit does not touch step_angular_speed. It stays vol.In([-180,-120,120,180]) (services.py:994-996), entirely inside the measured 120-180 band. The rule that comment states is honoured, not violated.

4. Nothing in the safety envelope depends on the yaw model being right at 300. Inside _step_response_probe_impl, linear_speed appears only in the new lower-bound travel table (services.py:10098-10105) and in the echoed result. Containment is step_path_contained (services.py:9644-9660), which demands max_travel_m + 0.50 m of clearance in EVERY direction — an explicitly curvature- and speed-independent disk — plus the in-window guard capping cumulative travel at 4.5 m. A path of cumulative length ≤ 4.5 m cannot leave a 5.0 m disk whatever shape the arc takes. So "yaw response at (300,180) differs from (400,180)" changes the curve, not the containment.

5. The consequence the claim describes is predeclared, not hidden. docs/phase2-long-step-slow-speed-predeclared-20260901.md:83-86, registered before any run and cited by the commit message: "linear_speed 300 is a different operating point, so results are NOT directly comparable to the four banked runs at 400, and the rotation rate at +180 may itself depend on linear speed — that is unmeasured. Do not merge this run into the n-count of the 400 runs." §4's outcome table also pre-assigns a reading to "2a FAIL with a large half_diff" ("a finding about the plant, not the statistic"). A run that returns an incomparable τ is a stated property of the experiment, not an undetected defect.

6. The k>=7 derivation does not rest on linear speed. Per docs/findings-plus180-split-is-onset-sampling-phase-20260901.md §3, k is the count of informative intervals in a half phase, set by the ~1 Hz VIO cadence and the step duration — neither is a function of the linear command. The real sensitivity there is the cadence tail, and the predeclaration's own §6.2 already corrects for it (slowest observed 1316 ms cadence gives k=5.70 and FAILS the bound) — i.e. the weakness the claim gestures at is registered from a different, correct direction.

7. Exposure is nil by accident: default stays 400 (services.py:986), and any non-dry run additionally needs confirm_step_response_run per call plus explicit operator authorization.

Residual, stated honestly: the code comment is thinner than the predeclaration — a reader of services.py alone sees "the objection does not transfer" without the "this is a new operating point" caveat that lives in the predeclaration and in a note pointing at the finding doc. That is a comment-completeness preference, not a correctness defect in this code, and it is one link away.

REFUTED. The arithmetic in the claim is correct (0.10 * 23 = 2.30 <= 2.50 default, so the blocker does not fire at linear 300 with default max_travel_m — confirmed by running _step_response_probe), but the conclusion does not follow, on four independently sufficient grounds.

(1) The gate's purpose is misstated. services.py:10092-10099 says verbatim: "A long window at the FAST speed overruns the distance guard mid-run... Refuse that pairing before dispatch." The predeclaration says the same. Linear 300 is the config that FITS the unchanged budget — that is why 300 was made admissible at all. The claim's headline ("the very config it exists to protect") inverts the code's own stated scope.

(2) "No discriminating power at 300" is false. The gate fires at 300 whenever max_travel_m < 2.30. Verified empirically: 300 / 3000+15000+5000 / max_travel_m 2.25 -> ['step_window_travel_exceeds_budget'].

(3) The commit reduces this hazard class rather than creating it. A window already legal BEFORE this commit — linear 400, 3000/7000/5000 = 15 s, default max_travel_m 2.50 — covers 3.92 m at the commit's own measured 0.2616 m/s and would trip the guard mid-run with no pre-dispatch refusal at all. That case now fires: verified 400 / 15 s / default 2.50 -> ['step_window_travel_exceeds_budget']. The "operator left max_travel_m at default, guard trips, run wasted" failure predates the commit and is now partially mitigated by it.

(4) The value 0.10 is a deliberate, documented LOWER bound (services.py:9529-9538: "Rounded DOWN on purpose, and that direction is the whole point... a merely MARGINAL config still dispatches and only an impossible one is refused"), with a separate constant named for the opposite rounding when sizing a corridor. The only 300 measurement (0.116 m/s) is a 4 s average including ramp and stop, n=1; treating it as an exact lower bound is less conservative than the gate's own contract requires. The claim's proposed direction (the ~0.159 m/s sustained estimate) would flip the gate to refusing merely-marginal configs — exactly the regression the commit reverted and pinned against in test_the_travel_refusal_does_not_tighten_the_existing_defaults (test_step_response_probe.py:797-813) — and would falsely refuse 300-speed windows above 15.7 s at the default budget that in fact cover only 1.82 m at the measured speed.

Consequence check: the claimed scenario requires the operator to deviate from the predeclared run (which fixes max_travel_m 4.5) on a call that already requires per-call confirm_step_response_run. The outcome is a travel-guard trip — a safe abort, scored FAIL by the predeclaration's own table. max_travel_m's 4.5 ceiling and step_path_contained's +0.50 m clearance are untouched, so no containment bound is affected. The cost is a wasted supervised run, which is precisely the class the code declares out of scope: "a marginal config is left to the guard, which is what actually carries the safety."

This is a disagreement with a documented, test-pinned design choice (an intentional false negative in a conservative filter), not a correctness defect in the code.

result.dimension: justifying arithmetic (half_diff onset model, interval budget at 15 s, speed table / travel extrapolation)

findings.title: half_diff model omits the residual term; a 15 s step is a ~59% coin flip, not a fix
findings.summary: `half_diff ≈ |steady − onset| / k` is structurally correct for the shipped endpoint-difference statistic but models ONLY the onset interval. Re-scoring all five banked runs through the shipped `_step_response_half_phase_agreement` with the shipped k = (N+1)//2 gives observed/predicted ratios of 1.34, 1.58, 0.09, 1.31, 1.50 — it under-predicts by 31–58% in four runs and over-predicts by 11x in the fifth (the only 2a PASS). The omitted term is not small: removing the onset interval entirely from the banked +180 run and re-scoring leaves half_diff = 1.625 °/s, still over the 1.5 bound, so half_diff does NOT tend to 0 as k grows. A bootstrap that draws the non-onset intervals from the 12 banked +180 ex-onset intervals (mean −12.14, sd 1.383 °/s; iid, so optimistic — real autocorrelation makes it worse) gives, at the worst observed onset (−1.35 °/s): step 15000 → 15 intervals, k=8, median half_diff 1.35, P(2a pass) = 58.5%; 14 intervals, k=7 → 47.7%. Even a 20 s step (k=10) only reaches 76%. Insensitive to dt modelling (fixed 0.995 s vs resampling the observed dt pool: 58.5% vs 58.8%). §6.2's corrected claim that 15000 ms 'passes by 8.1%' is the onset-only figure and does not hold.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator runs the authorized baseline 3000 / step 15000 / settle 5000, +180, linear 300 config. 2a comes back FAIL at half_diff ≈ 1.5–2.5 °/s roughly 40% of the time purely from residual scatter. §4's outcome table routes that to '2a FAIL with a large half_diff → The step is not steady even at 15 s — a finding about the plant, not the statistic', so a supervised motion run is spent and its result is written into the record as a plant finding when it is the statistic's own noise floor. Conversely a PASS (59%) is equally uninformative: the same bootstrap passes 58.5% of the time with no change in the plant at all.

findings.title: _STEP_RESPONSE_MIN_SPEED_BY_LINEAR[400] = 0.24 is not a lower bound; 4 of 5 banked runs are slower
findings.summary: The comment above the table (services.py:9529-9537) states it is 'Rounded DOWN on purpose … refuses only a window that overruns max_travel_m even at the slowest speed the mower has ever shown'. Measuring `cumulative_travel_m` (the guard's own metric, the exact quantity the blocker is proxying) over the full window of every banked linear-400 run gives 0.1934, 0.1969, 0.2085, 0.2133 and 0.2582 m/s — mean 0.2141, min 0.1934. The tabled 0.24 is 11–24% ABOVE four of the five, and was derived from the single fastest run (cited in the comment as '0.2616 m/s over a full 15 s window'). It is an upper-middle estimate wearing a lower-bound label, so the new `step_window_travel_exceeds_budget` blocker (services.py:10099-10106) over-refuses rather than, as its own comment claims, leaving marginal configs to the guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A follow-up run of baseline 3000 / step 12000 / settle 5000 (20000 ms) at linear 400, max_travel_m 4.5 — a configuration that needs no new operating point and no unmeasured slow-speed turn response — computes floor_travel_m = 0.24 × 20 = 4.8 > 4.5 and is refused pre-dispatch, although the four slower banked observations put actual travel at 3.87–4.28 m, inside the guard. Likewise, re-running the exact banked route-1 run-1 config (3000/5000/5000 = 13 s, linear 400) at a deliberately tightened max_travel_m of 3.0 is now refused (floor 3.12 > 3.0) even though both banked runs at that config travelled 2.71 m and 2.77 m.

findings.title: §2's 'the yard runs out at linear 400' rests on the single fastest of five speed observations
findings.summary: §2 derives 'max window at linear 400 ≈ 17.2 s → step ≤ ~10.2 s → worst-case half_diff 2.09, still FAILS' from one number, 0.2616 m/s, and never reports the 33% run-to-run spread in the same evidence set (0.1934–0.2582 m/s across five banked linear-400 runs at fixed commands). Recomputing 4.5 m / speed: at the mean 0.2141 m/s the max window is 21.0 s → step 13.0 s → 13 intervals → k=7, which is exactly the k §1 declares sufficient; at the slowest 0.1934 m/s a full 15 s step (23 s window, 4.45 m) fits at linear 400. So the premise that forces a NEW operating point is not established — and that operating point is one the document itself flags as unmeasured twice (§4: the +180 rotation rate at linear 300 'is unmeasured'; §6.1: 'There is NO sustained-speed measurement at linear 300 anywhere in the record').
findings.failure_scenario: The change admits linear 300 and the authorized run drives at it. If the +180 rotation rate is speed-dependent (unmeasured, and at linear 300 the commanded arc radius drops to roughly 0.6 m so the inner wheel sits far closer to the documented stationary actuation deadband), the resulting ω is not comparable to any of the four banked runs at 400 and the run cannot be merged with them — leaving n=1 at a config chosen on the strength of a speed figure that four of five same-command observations contradict, when a 12–13 s step at the already-characterised linear 400 would very likely have fitted.

findings.title: The model's only numerical verification uses a k the shipped code never produces
findings.summary: `_step_response_half_phase_agreement` builds N+1 readings, sets boundary = (N+1)//2, and takes readings[:boundary+1] as the first half — so the first half holds k = (N+1)//2 INTEGER intervals: k=4 for a 7-interval step, k=7 for 14, k=8 for 15. §1 verifies the model as '10.43/3.5 = 2.98 predicted vs 3.4049 observed', using k = N/2 = 3.5, a value the code cannot produce. With the code's own k=4 the prediction is 2.608 against 3.405 observed — 23% low, not the 12% the 3.5 figure implies. §6.2 repeats the same non-integer convention (k = 7.57 for a 15 s step). The verification is also single-point: applying the identical model to the other banked +180 run predicts 5.684/4 = 1.42 (or 1.62 at k=3.5) against 0.130 observed, an 11x miss on the run that PASSED, and the document does not report it.
findings.failure_scenario: A later session re-sizes a step from this model — e.g. computes '10.43/k ≤ 1.5 ⇒ k ≥ 7 ⇒ 14 intervals' — and gets 14 intervals, where the shipped statistic gives k=7 and worst-case 10.43/7 = 1.49 against a 1.5 bound: 0.7% of margin, not the 8.1% §6.2 quotes for k=7.57. The non-integer k systematically overstates the margin at every odd interval count, and the single-point fit hides that the model's sign of error is not consistent.

findings.title: '~5.9 m corridor' contradicts the containment gate the code actually enforces
findings.summary: §3 and §4 (line 70) size the corridor from predicted travel: '~2.5 m, needing only a ~5.9 m corridor … far more than the ~5.9 m required'. `_step_response_gates`'s `step_path_contained` (services.py:9640-9660) never consults predicted travel — it requires `polygon_boundary_clearance(live_position) >= max_travel_m + stop_overshoot_m` = 4.5 + 0.50 = 5.0 m in every direction, i.e. a 10.0 m square centred on the live position. §6.3 restates the 5.0 m requirement but does not retract the 5.9 m figure, so the document contradicts itself.
findings.failure_scenario: A session preparing the run scans and freezes a ~6 m corridor on the strength of §3/§4, positions the mower, and the dry run refuses with `step_path_contained` (clearance ≈ 3.0 m against required_radius_m 5.0). The obvious-looking recovery — dropping max_travel_m to ~2.45 so the gate passes — silently removes the guard headroom that §6.1's own corrected estimate of 3.65–3.7 m of travel needs, converting a corridor-sizing error into a mid-window guard trip and a censored measurement.

result.notes:
Answers to the three questions, from independent re-derivation using docs/raw-samples/ and the shipped `_step_response_vio_intervals` / `_step_response_half_phase_agreement` (extracted and run against all five banked runs).

(a) Model structure is RIGHT, calibration is WRONG. The shipped statistic is an endpoint-difference over each half (half_rate = Δheading/Δt between three readings only), so a rate deficit confined to interval 1 does contribute exactly (steady−onset)·dt_onset / T_firsthalf ≈ |steady−onset|/k. But the model has no residual term, and the residual is large: ex-onset half_diff, re-scored through the shipped function, is 1.625 (banked +180 — still FAILS the 1.5 bound with the onset gone), 0.107, 0.816, 2.084, 0.897. Observed/predicted ratios across the five runs: 1.34, 1.58, 0.09, 1.31, 1.50.

(b) A 15 s step DOES yield ≥14 intervals — but that is not enough. Measured VIO cadence: mean 982.9–996.6 ms per run (pooled 991 ms), median 1013–1019 ms, max gap 1316.5 ms. Every banked run's step phase produced exactly step_ms/1000 intervals (5000→5, 7000→7), so 15000→15 (k=8), 14 with jitter (k=7). Bootstrap over the 12 banked +180 ex-onset intervals: P(2a pass) = 58.5% at k=8 and 47.7% at k=7 with the worst observed onset (−1.35 °/s); 84% with the milder onset (−5.68). ~20 s of step (k=10) still only reaches 76%. So the change does not remove the sampling-phase coin flip it was written to remove — it improves it from ~12% to ~59%.

(c) 0.116 m/s is not trustworthy, and the document already self-corrects this in §6.1 (to ~0.159 m/s, ~3.65–3.7 m, ~81% of the budget) — I did not re-report that as a defect. My independent check: the 1.37x ramp-correction factor §6.1 uses is itself derived from the single fastest linear-400 run (0.191 → 0.2616). Against the mean of all five full-window linear-400 observations (0.2141) the factor is 1.12x, giving ~0.130 m/s and ~2.99 m. So the true range is ~3.0–3.7 m of a 4.5 m guard; a guard trip at linear 300 is possible but unlikely, and §6.1's warning is appropriately conservative. Two further points §6 does not make: cumulative_travel_m sums per-sample |chord|, so at 0.116–0.159 m/s with 2–4 cm position noise the guard reads ~5–8% high (conservative, trips early, ~0.2–0.3 m of phantom travel over 23 samples); and the repo's own deliberately-rounded-UP corridor-sizing constant `_PROBE_SPEED_PER_LINEAR_UNIT_MS` (services.py:904, 7.0e-04) predicts 0.21 m/s at linear 300 → 4.83 m over 23 s, which exceeds max_travel_m — the two speed models in this commit differ by 2.1x for linear 300 and only the optimistic one is cited.

Not defects, checked and cleared: the travel guard is cumulative path length (matching the blocker's speed×time model, not displacement); `total_ms` is the right multiplier since linear_speed is held for all three phases; heading wrap in `normalize_degrees` over a half is safe (≈94–117° per half at the observed +180 rates, vs a 180° limit); the 10.0 m corridor gives exactly the required 5.0 m clearance because the corridor is re-centred on the live position each run (confirmed from all five banked runs' `step_path_contained` diagnostics); and `test_the_travel_refusal_does_not_tighten_the_existing_defaults` correctly pins the 0.24 × 10 s = 2.4 ≤ 2.5 default case.
